title_topics: AI, IoT, Big Data and Augmented Reality — the Data-Driven Ship · Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technology in Shipping · 3D Printing and Additive Manufacturing
meta_description: MEO Class 1 Engineering Management Notes Part 31, the final Part — new technologies in shipping. AI defined (OECD and ISO/IEC 22989) and separated from automation, machine learning and Big Data; deployed vs demonstrated maritime AI; the Internet of Things, Big Data's five Vs and their uses in chartering, operations, vetting and design; augmented, virtual and mixed reality for remote maintenance and training. Then blockchain and distributed ledger technology: real properties (tamper-evident, permissioned, not private), electronic bills of lading and their legal basis (MLETR, UK ETDA 2023, India's Bills of Lading Act 2025), smart contracts and the oracle problem, fuel traceability and limits. Then 3D printing and additive manufacturing: ISO/ASTM 52900, process categories, and class qualification of printed parts (IACS Rec. 186, DNV AMC categories) — why a downloaded file is not a certified spare. Source PDF 741–764 + 768; PDF 765–767 belong to Part 27. Facts verified as of 8 October 2026. Originally compiled by Uday Sankar S., Anglo-Eastern.

topics.verify: Source range. PDF 741–745 and 753–764 (notebook 107–109 and 114–120) — items 1 (AI), III (Augmented Reality), IV (IoT) and V (Big Data) of Uday's chapter Maritime Industry & incorporation of New technologies. Item 2 (Blockchain, 746–752) is Topic 2. Source errors corrected. (1) AI definition (P31-C001): 'the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines' is popular wording; replaced by the OECD (2023) / ISO/IEC 22989 definition. (2) 'AI works by ingesting labelled training data' describes supervised machine learning, not all AI (P31-C003); AI ≠ ML ≠ automation ≠ Big Data. (3) 'Three types of AI as stages' (P31-C007): only narrow AI exists; AGI and ASI are hypothetical, and superintelligence is not 'machine consciousness'. Cortana's Windows app was retired in 2023. (4) 'Automated container loading' and Rotterdam's automated terminals are mainly fixed-logic automation, not AI (P31-C011, C015). (5) Automation does not remove human error — it moves it (P31-C014). (6) The insurer claims (lower premium, AI fraud detection) could not be verified for marine insurers and are removed (P31-C017, UNVERIFIED). (7) VR: 'user need not be present' and the unsourced '2–4 year adoption horizon' are removed (P31-C048, C049). (8) Big Data: volume alone does not define it, and velocity is the speed of generation and processing, not 'growth' (P31-C067, C069). (9) Shipping's GHG share is about 2.9% (2018, Fourth IMO GHG Study), not 2% (P31-C071). (10) IMO target: net-zero GHG 'by or around, i.e. close to, 2050' with 2030 and 2040 checkpoints — and the Net-Zero Framework is not yet adopted (P31-C072). Deployed vs demonstrated is labelled for every named example; all are dated as of 8 October 2026 and none is a memory item.
topics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI): a machine-based system that, for given objectives, infers from its input how to generate outputs — predictions, recommendations or decisions — that influence a physical or virtual environment (OECD, 2023). Machine learning is the main AI technique today: models learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects sensors and devices so that data flows automatically to processing and users (ITU-T Y.2060). Big Data is data whose volume, velocity and variety need scalable methods to store and analyse (NIST SP 1500-1). Augmented reality (AR) overlays computer-generated information on the user's view of the real world in real time; virtual reality replaces that view entirely. Together they make the data-driven ship: IoT collects the data, Big Data stores it, AI finds patterns in it, and AR puts the result in front of the engineer.
why: Simon asks for definitions that hold up. 'What is AI?' answered with 'computers thinking like humans' invites the follow-up 'So is your governor AI?' Know that AI ≠ automation ≠ machine learning ≠ Big Data.

The engine room is where most of this lands. Condition monitoring, maker anomaly-detection services, reefer monitoring and AR remote assistance are already in service — and every one of them is a connection into OT (Part 30).
Deployed or demonstrated? An examiner who reads trade press will know that a famous autonomous voyage was a demonstration and that terminal automation is not AI. Present examples honestly and dated.
The CE stays accountable. AI flags and AR guidance assist; they never remove a statutory survey, override watchkeeping judgement or replace the SMS.

sections.head: 🧠 AI — Definition, and What It Is Not

body.p: Uday's opening line is popular-press wording. The definition to give is the OECD's (2023), mirrored in ISO/IEC 22989: an AI system is a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs — predictions, content, recommendations or decisions — that can influence physical or virtual environments.

head: Term
What it is
Engine-room example
rows: Automation
Fixed logic written by an engineer: same input, same output
PID governor, auxiliary-engine auto-start, alarm and safety shutdowns
Machine learning (ML)
A subset of AI: a model learns patterns from data; Uday's 'labelled training data' describes supervised ML
Anomaly detection trained on months of normal engine data
AI
The wider field — ML plus rule-based reasoning, optimisation and language models
A decision-support tool that ranks probable causes of a high exhaust temperature
Big Data
The raw material — very large, fast, varied data sets; not intelligence by itself
Fleet-wide sensor archives

body.p: Learning, reasoning, self-correction. Uday's 'three cognitive skills' is a teaching description, not a standard. In practice, 'self-correction' means a model is retrained or updated on new data — on board that is a managed software change, not autonomous self-improvement. And in ML the algorithm that trains the model is written by people, but the model's rules are learned.

'Three types of AI'. Every AI system in use today, maritime or otherwise, is narrow AI, built for one task. General AI (human-level across all tasks) and super-intelligence are hypothetical, and super-intelligence is not 'machine consciousness'. Uday's Cortana example is dated: Microsoft retired the Windows app in 2023.

body.p: Pros and cons — the CE's version. Uday's lists hold (better analytics, route optimisation, maintenance optimisation; poor data quality, unclear strategy, job fears). Add four cons he leaves out: cyber exposure of every connected system (Part 30); limited explainability ('why did it flag this?'); over-reliance and de-skilling of watchkeepers; and dependence on sensor quality and connectivity. Automation does not remove human error — it moves it into design, configuration, sensors and the interface.

Class. Class societies do offer digital services: electronic certificates, remote surveys (IACS UR Z29 for surveys from 1 January 2023) and smart or digital notations (DNV Smart, ABS SMART, LR Digital). His three challenges stand — cyber security, the highest levels of autonomy, and initial cost.

body.p: Uday's four parts are a fair teaching model (ITU-T Y.2060 is the formal reference; Simon Notes Part 4 · Note 31 uses six 'pillars'). One correction matters on a ship: IoT that 'automatically adjusts the devices without the user' would mean writing commands into OT from shore. Most shipboard IoT is read-only monitoring, and any write-back into machinery control needs an approved design, onboard acceptance and the remote-access controls of Part 30 (IACS UR E26 on new ships).

sections.head: 📊 Big Data — the 5 Vs and Their Uses

head: V
Meaning (corrected)
Ship example

Quantity of data too large for ordinary tools — volume alone does not define big data
Years of one-second engine and fuel-flow data across a fleet
Velocity
Speed at which data is generated and must be processed (not 'growth')
Continuous sensor streams; AIS position reports

body.p: The original three Vs (volume, velocity, variety) are Doug Laney's, META Group, 2001; veracity and value were added later, so '5 Vs' is a teaching convention. Simon Notes Part 4 · Note 30 covers the same list.

Uses (Uday's four, confirmed). Chartering — matching the right ship to the cargo at the right price. Operations — the optimum economic speed. Vetting — charterers select ships on inspection and performance data (OCIMF SIRE 2.0 went live on 2 September 2024). Ship design — operating data from existing ships informs new designs. Challenges: data processing, connectivity and data security.

Regulation as the driver — figures corrected. Shipping produced about 2.9% of global anthropogenic GHG emissions in 2018 (2.76% in 2012; Fourth IMO GHG Study 2020), not 2%. IMO's 2023 Strategy targets net-zero GHG emissions 'by or around, i.e. close to, 2050', with checkpoints of at least 20% (striving for 30%) by 2030 and 70% (striving for 80%) by 2040, against 2008. The measure meant to deliver it, the IMO Net-Zero Framework, was not adopted as of 8 October 2026: adoption was adjourned in October 2025, and it is due for consideration at MEPC 85 (30 November–3 December 2026) and the resumed extraordinary session (4 December 2026). Verified fuel data is what DCS, CII and any future pricing measure all depend on.

body.p: AR ≠ VR. Uday's line that in VR the 'user need not be present' is removed — the user is fully immersed; it is the real surroundings that disappear. His '2–4 year time horizon for VR adoption' has no traceable source and is removed.

The maritime example he cites is real. Wärtsilä Seals & Bearings announced smart-glasses remote support for stern-tube (S/T) work on 31 July 2018; MAN Energy Solutions (now Everllence) piloted its PrimeServ EyeTech assisted-reality service from December 2019. Simon Notes Part 6 describes the same Wärtsilä use. Class societies also run remote surveys by video (IACS UR Z29).

ce_tip.text: Simon asks, 'What is AI, and is it used on your ship?' Give the definition in one sentence — a machine-based system that infers from its input how to produce predictions, recommendations or decisions — then draw the line: 'My governor is automation; the maker's anomaly-detection service that learns my engine's normal behaviour is machine learning, which is a kind of AI.' Name one deployed example and one demonstration, and say which is which. If he asks about AR, define it against VR in one line each and give the stern-tube smart-glasses example. Close with control: 'Every one of these is a connection into OT, so it sits under our cyber procedures — and none of it replaces a survey or my judgement.'

qa: Q1. Define artificial intelligence. How does it differ from automation and from machine learning?

An AI system is a machine-based system that, for given objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations or decisions that influence a physical or virtual environment — that is the OECD definition of 2023, close to ISO/IEC 22989. Automation is fixed logic designed by an engineer: a governor, an auto-start sequence or a safety shutdown gives the same output for the same input and learns nothing. Machine learning is the main branch of AI in use today: instead of hand-written rules, a model learns patterns from data — supervised learning from labelled examples, unsupervised learning from unlabelled data. Big data is different again: it is the raw material that machine learning works on. All AI in use today is narrow AI, built for a specific task; general AI and super-intelligence are hypothetical.
Q2. Give examples of how AI is being used in shipping, distinguishing deployed systems from demonstrations.

Deployed: port-call optimisation that predicts arrival and berth times so that ships can arrive just in time; weather routing and performance models refined by machine learning for fuel optimisation; maker anomaly-detection services that learn an engine's normal behaviour and flag deviations, such as Wärtsilä's Expert Insight; and computer-vision collision-avoidance aids used as decision support on the bridge. Demonstrated: autonomous ocean voyages such as HD Hyundai's trans-Pacific HiNAS voyage of the Prism Courage in 2022 and Japan's MEGURI 2040 trials. Automated container terminals, such as those in Rotterdam since 1993, are mainly fixed-logic automation, not AI. Autonomous ships are regulated only by IMO's non-mandatory MASS Code, effective 1 July 2026.
Q3. What is the Internet of Things? Give its main parts and its advantages and disadvantages on board.

The Internet of Things is a network of physical devices — sensors and actuators with embedded electronics — connected so that their data flows automatically, without human data entry, to processing and to users. Its main parts are the sensors or devices, the connectivity (ship network and satellite link), the data processing, on board or in the cloud, and the user interface such as a dashboard or alarm. Advantages: efficiency and cost reduction, real-time information, better decisions from analytics, predictive maintenance and fuel saving; examples include hull and machinery condition monitoring and reefer monitoring. Disadvantages: cost, technical complexity, dependence on technology, connectivity and power, integration with existing systems — and above all security risk, because every IoT link is a path into the ship's operational technology, so it must be segmented and controlled.
Q4. What is Big Data? Explain its characteristics and its uses in ship management.

Big data is data whose volume, velocity and variety are too great for conventional tools, so that scalable methods are needed to store and analyse it. The five Vs used in teaching are volume, the quantity of data; velocity, the speed at which it is generated and must be processed; variety, the different types such as sensor values, reports and images; veracity, its trustworthiness; and value, the usefulness of the insight relative to the cost. The original three Vs are Doug Laney's from 2001. Uses include chartering — matching the right ship to the cargo at the right price; operations — finding the optimum economic speed; vetting — charterers selecting ships on inspection and performance data; and ship design, using operating data from existing ships. Regulation is a driver: shipping produced about 2.9 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions in 2018, and IMO's 2023 Strategy targets net-zero GHG by or around 2050, which needs verified fuel and performance data.
Q5. Differentiate augmented, virtual and mixed reality, and explain how AR helps the engine room.

Augmented reality overlays computer-generated information on the user's view of the real world in real time; Azuma's three characteristics are that it combines real and virtual, is interactive in real time and is registered in three dimensions. Virtual reality replaces the view of the real world with a fully synthetic environment. Mixed reality blends real and virtual objects so that they interact. In the engine room, AR lets a shore technician see what the engineer sees through smart glasses and guide him step by step — Wärtsilä introduced this for stern-tube seal work in 2018 — which reduces downtime and service visits; it also supports remote class surveys and maintenance instructions overlaid on the machine. VR is mainly used for training and drills ashore. The challenges are cost, latency, information overload, the need for intrinsically safe devices in hazardous areas, and cyber security, because the remote-assistance link is a form of remote vendor access.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — When the Algorithm Flags the Main Engine
blocks: The maker's remote-monitoring service e-mails an alert: 'Unit 4 — abnormal exhaust temperature trend; recommend inspection within 48 hours.' All readings on the ship's alarm system are inside limits.
How the Chief Engineer handles it

Verify, don't obey. The alert is decision support from a model that learned the engine's normal pattern; cross-check it against your own instruments, the indicator diagrams or engine-diagnostic data, recent fuel analysis and the scavenge-port inspection. Check the data first. A drifting thermocouple is the commonest cause of a 'trend' — veracity before intelligence. Decide and record. If the evidence supports it, plan the inspection under the PMS; if not, record why the alert was not acted on. Feedback. Tell the maker the outcome, so that the model improves. Boundaries. The alert cannot defer a class survey or replace the planned maintenance a condition-monitoring notation still requires; the remote link to the maker must sit inside the ship's cyber procedures (Part 30).
AI moves the engineer from collecting data to judging it. The value lies in earlier warning; the risk lies in trusting it blindly — or in ignoring it because nobody understood why it flagged.

topics.verify: Source range. PDF 746–752 (notebook 110–113) — item 2 of Uday's new-technologies chapter; PDF 748 carries a pasted printed CFTE diagram (centralised vs decentralised ledger), described but not reproduced. Source errors corrected. (1) Definition (P31-C020): blocks, hash links, signatures and consensus added (NIST IR 8202). (2) 'Six principles' (P31-C021) is not a recognised list; replaced by the defining properties. (3) 'Free of hacks and frauds', 'no single stakeholder can close the chain' and 'all participants make decisions' are overstated (P31-C022, C023, C025) — TradeLens was closed by its two owners. (4) 'Inclusive' is true only of public chains; shipping uses permissioned ledgers (P31-C026). (5) REMOVE — privacy (P31-C027): hashing is not encryption, public chains are pseudonymous and visible, and privacy is a limitation (as Uday's own challenge 7 says). (6) 'Smart B/L' → electronic bill of lading; its legal effect comes from law or a platform rulebook, not from blockchain; India's Bills of Lading Act 2025 does not mention electronic B/Ls (P31-C034). (7) Smart contracts need trusted outside data — the oracle problem (P31-C035). (8) OUTDATED — fuel traceability (P31-C036): only trials (BunkerTrace, 2019); Singapore's e-BDN is digital, not blockchain. (9) Energy depends on consensus — proof of stake and permissioned ledgers use little (P31-C038). (10) Sustainability: savings come from data sharing and just-in-time arrival, not from blockchain itself; shipping's GHG share is about 2.9%, not 2% (P31-C041–C043). topics.definition: A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks, each carrying a cryptographic hash of the previous block and signed by its originator, and copies of the ledger held by many nodes are kept in step by a consensus mechanism, usually without a central authority. The result is tamper-evident: changing a past record breaks the chain of hashes and is visible to the other nodes. Distributed ledger technology (DLT) is the wider family — every blockchain is a DLT, but not every DLT uses chained blocks. In shipping, DLT is used mainly on permissioned platforms for electronic trade documents, above all the electronic bill of lading (eBL).
why: Nair asks about the law, not the code. 'Is an electronic B/L valid?' is answered with MLETR, national statutes and the P&I-approved platform rulebook — not with 'it's on blockchain'.
Hype is the trap. 'Immutable', 'hack-proof' and 'private' are the three words examiners use to catch candidates who learnt blockchain from marketing.
Real projects have failed. TradeLens, the flagship shipping blockchain, closed in 2023. Knowing what is current and what is historical shows judgement.
The CE meets it at the bunker manifold. Digital bunker documentation (e-BDN) is now mandatory in Singapore — and it is not blockchain; the MARPOL sample still proves the fuel.

body.p: Uday's definition — a digital ledger distributed among the nodes of a peer-to-peer network rather than held in one central database — is the right starting point; his sketch of chained boxes shows the idea. What makes it a blockchain is the rest: transactions grouped into blocks, each block carrying the hash of the one before, digital signatures proving who submitted each record, and a consensus rule deciding which new block all nodes accept. NIST calls blockchains 'tamper evident and tamper resistant digital ledgers implemented in a distributed fashion'.

DLT and blockchain. Uday's 'tree and branch' is correct: every blockchain is a DLT, but some DLTs do not chain blocks. The pasted CFTE diagram on PDF 748 contrasts a centralised ledger, with one bank holding the record, against a decentralised ledger, where every party holds a synchronised copy.

sections.head: 🔍 Uday's 'Six Principles' — Tested Against the Evidence

head: Uday's principle
Verdict
What to say instead
rows: Decentralisation — 'no single stakeholder can hack, manipulate or close the chain; free of hacks and frauds'
Overstated

No single point of control or failure for the ledger. But 51% attacks, smart-contract bugs and stolen keys happen; consortium platforms can be closed by their owners (TradeLens, 2023); and false data entered at the start stays false.
Integrity — 'all participants have the right to make decisions'
Wrong for shipping
Integrity comes from hash-linking plus consensus; in permissioned ledgers only authorised nodes validate.
Cryptography — 'fair to all'
Half right
Hashing for integrity and public-key signatures for authenticity; 'fair to all' has no technical meaning.
Security — 'no central point of failure'
Partly right
No single database to attack; security still depends on key management, endpoints and code.
Inclusive — 'everyone can participate'
Only for public chains
Permissionless chains are open to anyone; shipping platforms admit vetted members only.
'Respects your privacy — hash-key encryption, identity not disclosed'
Wrong — removed

Hashing is not encryption. Public chains are pseudonymous and every transaction is visible. Confidential data is kept off-chain or on permissioned ledgers, with only hashes on the chain. Privacy is a limitation.

body.p: The defining properties to learn: distributed ledger · consensus · cryptographic hash-linking (tamper-evident, append-only) · digital signatures · permissionless vs permissioned. Say 'very hard to alter undetected', not 'immutable'.

body.p: 'Blockchain helps sustainability' — the causal chain corrected. Uday's figures need updating: shipping carries over 80% of world goods trade by volume (UNCTAD; the industry says around 90%), and it produced about 2.9% of global GHG emissions in 2018 (Fourth IMO GHG Study), not 2%. Emissions are saved when ships stop hurrying to wait at anchor — just-in-time arrival, which IMO's 2020 JIT Arrival Guide shows depends on shared, trusted port-call data. Blockchain is one possible way to share such data; the saving comes from the data sharing and the slower steaming, not from the ledger.

ce_tip.text: Nair asks, 'What is blockchain, and is a blockchain B/L valid?' Define it in one breath — a distributed ledger of hash-linked, signed blocks kept in step by consensus, tamper-evident rather than tamper-proof — then turn to the law: 'An electronic B/L is valid where the law recognises electronic transferable records, as under the UNCITRAL Model Law, enacted in the UK in 2023 and Singapore in 2021, or by contract through the platform's rulebook; it must be an International Group-approved system for P&I cover. Blockchain is only the technology; the validity comes from the law.' If he presses on India, say the Bills of Lading Act 2025 does not address electronic bills, so an Indian eBL rests on contract. Never call blockchain 'immutable' or 'private' — and mention that TradeLens closed in 2023.

qa: Q1. What is blockchain? How does it differ from distributed ledger technology in general?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks; each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block and digitally signed records, and many nodes hold copies that are kept identical by a consensus mechanism, usually without a central authority. Because each block depends on the hash of the one before, altering an old record breaks the chain and is evident to the other nodes, so the ledger is tamper-evident and very hard to alter undetected rather than absolutely immutable. Distributed ledger technology is the wider family of synchronised, consensus-based ledgers held across several sites; every blockchain is a DLT, but not every DLT chains its records in blocks. Ledgers are either permissionless and open to anyone, like Bitcoin, or permissioned, where only vetted members participate — the usual model in shipping.
Q2. Is blockchain secure and private? Comment on the common claims made for it.

It is secure against one specific threat — undetected alteration of the shared record — because of hash-linking, signatures and consensus, and it removes a single central database as a point of failure. It is not hack-proof: attacks on the consensus, faulty smart-contract code, stolen private keys and compromised user devices all occur, and if false data is entered at the start, the ledger faithfully preserves it. It is not inherently private: hashing is not encryption, and a public blockchain is pseudonymous, with every transaction visible to everyone, which is why commercial data is usually kept off-chain or on permissioned ledgers with only hashes recorded. It is not 'free of fraud' or impossible to close down: the flagship shipping platform TradeLens was shut down by its two owners in 2023.
Q3. What is an electronic bill of lading, and what gives it legal validity?

An electronic bill of lading is a digital record that performs the functions of a paper bill — receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage and document of title — with 'possession' transferred by passing exclusive control of the record on a platform. Its legal validity does not come from the technology but from the law or from contract. Where a country has adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records, as the UK did in its Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 and Singapore in 2021, an eBL can have the same effect as paper. Elsewhere it depends on a contractual rulebook binding all users of the platform. The International Group of P&I Clubs covers liabilities arising from eBLs only on systems it has approved. India has not enacted the Model Law, and the Bills of Lading Act 2025 does not mention electronic bills, so an Indian eBL rests on contract. Some approved platforms use blockchain and others do not.
Q4. What is a smart contract? Give a shipping example and its limitations.

A smart contract is code recorded on a blockchain that executes automatically when defined conditions are met. A shipping example is releasing a freight payment, or starting demurrage, when a verified arrival event is recorded. Its limitations are that it can only act on data it is given, so it needs a trusted source of real-world events — the oracle problem: if the arrival time fed in is wrong, the contract executes wrongly; the code can contain errors that are hard to correct once deployed; and its legal enforceability depends on an underlying legal contract, not on the code itself. In shipping, smart contracts remain at pilot stage.
Q5. What are the challenges in implementing blockchain in shipping?

Cost and initial investment; the need for every trading partner to join, since a ledger with one participant is worthless — the network effect that led to TradeLens closing in 2023; immaturity, scalability and lack of interoperability between platforms; governance — who runs the network and decides the rules; the oracle problem of feeding trustworthy data; legal recognition of electronic records, which varies by country; private-key management; data privacy, because public ledgers are transparent; and training. Energy consumption is a problem mainly for proof-of-work chains; proof-of-stake and permissioned ledgers use little energy.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — The eBL That Arrived Before the Ship
blocks: A container ship arrives at an Asian port. The receiver presents no paper bill but asks the agent to release the cargo against an 'electronic B/L on the blockchain platform'. The master is unsure and asks the Chief Engineer, the senior officer on board familiar with the company's digital systems, to help check.

Was the B/L issued electronically by the carrier? The eBL must be on the platform named in the bill and the charter party. Is the platform approved? Delivery against an eBL issued on a system not approved by the International Group may prejudice P&I cover — the company's instructions decide. Who holds exclusive control? The platform shows the current holder; delivery is only to that party. Which law applies? Where MLETR-based law applies, the eBL is treated like paper; otherwise the platform's rulebook binds the parties. The fact that the platform runs on blockchain proves the record's integrity, not the receiver's right to the cargo.
The technology answers 'has this record been altered?'; the law and the contract answer 'who owns the cargo?'. Delivery decisions stay with the master and the company under the SMS.

topics.definition: Additive manufacturing (AM) — commonly called 3D printing — is 'the process of joining materials to make parts from 3D model data, usually layer upon layer, as opposed to subtractive and formative manufacturing methodologies' (ISO/ASTM 52900:2021). A printed part is only as good as its qualified process: the feedstock, the machine and its parameters, the post-processing and the inspection. A printed part used where a classed or safety-critical component is required must therefore come from a class-qualified manufacturer with a part certificate, exactly as a cast or forged part would — a digital file alone is not a certified spare.
why: Spares at sea are the CE's problem. AM promises faster spares for obsolete or remote-port items. The CE must know which parts that promise applies to.
Paul asks about certification. 'Can you print a spare on board?' tests whether the candidate knows class approval, material certificates and the critical/non-critical distinction.
The risk is invisible. A printed part can look perfect and hide porosity, lack of fusion or residual stress. Only a qualified process and inspection prove it.
OEM rights are real. Printing a maker's part without a licence raises intellectual-property, warranty and liability questions.

How

body.p: The seven ISO/ASTM 52900 process categories: binder jetting, directed energy deposition (DED, including wire-arc additive manufacturing, WAAM), material extrusion, material jetting, powder bed fusion (PBF), sheet lamination and vat photopolymerisation. For marine metal parts the relevant routes are powder bed fusion for small, complex parts and DED/WAAM for large parts such as propellers; IACS Rec. 186 also covers binder jetting.

sections.head: 🏛️ Class Qualification — Why a File Is Not a Spare

body.p: There is no IACS Unified Requirement on AM yet. Class societies apply their own rules, harmonised by IACS Recommendation 186 (March 2025, non-mandatory), which sets three AM levels of testing according to the criticality of the part. DNV, for example, grades AM parts AMC 1 to AMC 3 by consequence of failure; its certificates state that categories 2 and 3 need part qualification on top of build-process qualification. The common elements:

head: What is qualified
Why
rows: The manufacturer / AM facility (Approval of Manufacturer)
Quality system, trained operators, calibrated machines
The feedstock — powder or wire
Chemistry, particle size, reuse limits, traceability
The build process — machine, parameters, orientation, post-processing
The same file on a different machine or settings gives a different part
The part — dimensional checks, NDT (often CT), mechanical test coupons
Detects porosity, lack of fusion, cracks
The digital file — revision control, licence, secure transfer
The right design, unaltered, legally used

head: Part type
Examples
Route

Pressure-retaining, rotating, propulsion and steering parts; anything under class survey
Class-approved AM manufacturer, qualified material and process, part certificate — the same standard as a cast or forged part
Non-critical
Knobs, covers, brackets, scupper plugs, tool holders
Lower risk, but still under the SMS (management of change), with the OEM's agreement where the design is the OEM's

sections.head: 🚢 Onboard Printing vs Shore Hubs — Practice in 2026

body.p: Merchant practice is shore-based. Verified commercial examples are parts printed at qualified facilities ashore and delivered to the ship — e.g. Wilhelmsen's printed scupper plugs for Berge Bulk (February 2020), later through a joint venture with thyssenkrupp — the 'digital warehouse' model, in which OEM-licensed build files are held digitally and printed at a qualified hub near the port.

Onboard metal printing is not merchant practice. It needs controlled powder handling, inert gas, heat treatment, inspection and trained operators, and ship motion and vibration affect the build — the US Navy itself cites motion and vibration limits for the metal printer it installed on USS Bataan in November 2022. A small polymer printer on board can make jigs, gauges and non-critical items, under the SMS. A 2017 industry proposal for onboard polymer printers on merchant ships is not known to have been taken further.

Intellectual property. Most machinery parts are the maker's design. Printing one without a licence can infringe design rights, void the warranty and leave the owner carrying the liability if it fails. OEM-licensed files through an approved hub avoid this.

ce_tip.text: Paul asks, 'Your fuel-pump part is obsolete — can you 3D-print it on board?' Answer: 'Not if it is a classed or safety-critical part. It must come from a class-approved additive-manufacturing facility, with qualified powder or wire, a qualified build process, heat treatment, NDT and a part certificate — the same standard as a cast or forged spare — and with the maker's licence for the design. IACS Recommendation 186 of March 2025 sets testing levels by criticality; DNV grades parts AMC 1 to 3. On board I can print only non-critical items, under the SMS.' If he asks for the definition, give ISO/ASTM 52900: joining materials layer by layer from 3D model data. Never say 'download the file and print it'.

qa: Q1. What is additive manufacturing, and how does it differ from conventional manufacturing?

Additive manufacturing, commonly called 3D printing, is defined in ISO/ASTM 52900 as the process of joining materials to make parts from 3D model data, usually layer upon layer. Conventional manufacturing is either subtractive — removing material from a solid, as when a bore is machined out of a billet — or formative — shaping material by casting or forging. Additive manufacturing uses little more material than the part itself and can make complex internal shapes that cannot be machined, but the properties of the part depend heavily on the process: a printed metal part can be anisotropic, porous or carry residual stress unless the process is qualified and the part is heat-treated and inspected, so it is not automatically cheaper or stronger.
Q2. Describe the steps in producing an engineering part by additive manufacturing.

First, a 3D CAD model of the part is obtained, under licence if the design belongs to the maker. Second, the build is prepared: the part is oriented, support structures added and the model sliced into thin layers by software. Third, it is printed layer by layer on a qualified machine with controlled feedstock — polymer filament, metal powder or wire, depending on the process. Fourth, it is post-processed: supports removed, heat-treated or hot isostatically pressed to relieve stress and close porosity, and machined to final dimensions. Fifth, it is inspected and tested — dimensional checks, non-destructive testing such as CT scanning, and mechanical tests on coupons. Finally, where the part is classed or critical, it is certified by the classification society.
Q3. Can a Chief Engineer print a spare part on board? Discuss.

For a classed or safety-critical component, no. Such a part must be made by a manufacturer approved by the classification society, with qualified feedstock and a qualified build process, post-processing, non-destructive testing and a part certificate, to the same standard as a cast or forged replacement. IACS Recommendation 186 of March 2025 sets the level of testing by the part's criticality, and DNV, ABS, Lloyd's Register, Bureau Veritas and ClassNK have their own rules. The design usually belongs to the maker, so a licence is needed, and printing it without one raises intellectual-property, warranty and liability issues. Metal printing on board is impractical: powder handling, inert gas, heat treatment, inspection and ship motion all work against it. A small polymer printer on board can produce non-critical items such as covers, knobs or tool holders under the SMS. The practical route for critical spares is a shore hub printing an OEM-licensed file under class approval.
Q4. What do classification societies qualify before accepting an additively manufactured part?

They qualify the manufacturer or AM facility, through an approval of manufacturer covering its quality system, machines and operators; the feedstock, its chemistry, particle size, reuse and traceability; the build process, meaning the machine, parameters, orientation and post-processing, because the same file on different settings gives a different part; and the part itself, through dimensional checks, non-destructive testing and mechanical testing of coupons. They also expect control of the digital file. The depth of qualification depends on criticality: IACS Recommendation 186 uses three levels, and DNV grades parts AMC 1 to AMC 3 by the consequence of failure.
Q5. Give examples of additive manufacturing in the marine industry.

Demonstrations and first approvals include the RAMLAB and Damen 'WAAMpeller', a wire-arc printed ship propeller tested with Bureau Veritas witnessing in November 2017, and DNV's first approval of an additive-manufacturing manufacturer, thyssenkrupp, in August 2019. In commercial use, Wilhelmsen delivered printed scupper plugs — non-critical parts — to a Berge Bulk carrier in February 2020, and ABS approved printed parts after a six-month in-service trial on the tanker Polar Endeavour in November 2021. In naval use, the US Navy installed a metal printer on USS Bataan in 2022. IACS published Recommendation 186 on additively manufactured metallic parts in March 2025. These are dated examples; the principle to remember is qualification and certification by criticality.

A supplier offers to 3D-print an obsolete fuel-pump component from a scanned sample and deliver it to the ship within two days. As Chief Engineer, discuss (a) the technical risks of the printed part, (b) the class, OEM and SMS requirements you would apply, and (c) when such a part may and may not be accepted.

Memory aid: model → prep → print → POST-PROCESS → INSPECT → CERTIFY. The last three make it safe.
Marine metal AM = PBF (small, complex) + DED/WAAM (large — propellers).
CRITICAL part = class-approved manufacturer + qualified feedstock and process + NDT + part certificate + OEM licence. IACS Rec. 186 (Mar 2025) · DNV AMC 1–3.
NEVER 'download and print' a classed spare. Merchant practice = qualified SHORE hub ('digital warehouse'); onboard = non-critical polymer only.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — The Obsolete Fuel-Pump Part
blocks: A small cast-steel part inside a main-engine fuel pump has cracked. The maker has discontinued it, and the lead time for a cast replacement is ten weeks. A supplier offers to scan the broken part and 3D-print a metal replacement within two days.

Classify the part. It is in a fuel-injection pump, so it is safety-critical and within class scope. Design right. Ask the maker for a licensed build file, or for its own AM or alternative supply route; a scan of a worn, cracked part is not a valid design. Class route. Any printed replacement must come from a class-approved AM facility, with qualified material and process, heat treatment, NDT and a part certificate accepted by the ship's class society. Interim. Meanwhile, run on the remaining pumps if the engine design and class allow, inform the superintendent and class, and record the deviation under the SMS. Reject the two-day offer if it cannot show facility approval and part certification.

Additive manufacturing can shorten the lead time for a critical spare — but only through the same qualification and certification chain as any other manufacturing route. Speed never replaces the certificate.
